title: Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Roles
summary: This sub-technique of account manipulation covers raising the privileges attached to a cloud identity so that the adversary keeps broad access to a tenant or subscription. In practice it means editing permission policies or attaching a new policy version, binding an existing policy to a compromised user or role, and assigning administrative directory roles such as a global administrator. A single well-chosen role can carry near total control over data and settings, including the ability to reset other administrators' passwords, which makes the change far more valuable than the compromise that preceded it. The same pattern appears in container platforms, where cloud role assignments may be used alongside local cluster permissions. Attackers may grant the new rights to an account they created, to a valid account they already control, or in some cases to an identity outside the victim tenant so that no victim owned account needs to be touched. Detection is driven by identity audit logs: role assignment and policy change events, policy versions that appear outside a deployment pipeline, privilege grants made by a principal that rarely performs them, and short sequences of account creation followed by permission change.

beginner.definition: This is a sub-technique of account manipulation. It means an attacker gives a cloud account more power than it should have, for example making it a global administrator. The account keeps that power until someone notices and removes it. It is one of the fastest ways to turn a small foothold into full control.
beginner.whyItMatters: A powerful cloud role can reach almost every file, setting and user in the company. With it, an attacker can reset other administrators' passwords, which makes removal much harder. Because the change is made through normal admin tools, it can look like routine work if nobody reviews role changes.
howItWorks: The attacker gets an account that is allowed to change permissions in the cloud tenant.
They attach an existing policy with wide rights to a user or service account they control.
Or they create a new version of a policy that quietly adds extra permissions.
They may also assign a directory role such as global administrator to that account.
Sometimes they grant the rights to an account in a different tenant they already own.
The cloud writes an audit event for each assignment, naming the actor and the target.
beginner.example: Picture a building where most staff hold a key to their own floor. A contractor copies the building manager's signature onto a form and gives a colleague a master key. The colleague never broke a door and never touched a lock. They simply walked into any room they liked, and the key list still showed their name.
takeaways: Alert on role assignment and permission policy changes, because they are high value events.
Know which accounts are allowed to grant privileges, and treat everything else as suspicious.
New accounts that gain power soon after creation deserve immediate review.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent account manipulation technique.
Describe how permission policies and administrative roles are changed in cloud environments.
Identify the identity audit events that record role and policy changes.
Distinguish routine deployment activity from adversary privilege granting.
Explain why privilege granting inside a tenant is so difficult to reverse.
